claims.claim: Someone who abandons the faith under pressure, or commits a grave sin, and comes back truly sorry, should be received back into the church.

stances.summary: The fallen who repent with their whole heart must be taken back into the Church after a real penance. Shutting the door drives them to despair, and no one can repent in the grave.
stances.quote: they who have repented from their whole heart, and have asked for it, ought to be received within the Church, and to be kept in it for the Lord, who will of a surety judge, when He comes to His Church, those whom He shall find within it.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: Letter 51, to Antonianus (Letter 55 in modern numbering)
stances.context: Written 251-252 after the Decian persecution, defending the African council's policy against Novatian. Cyprian changed course and explains it in this same letter (sections 3-7): early in 250 he refused to settle the case of the lapsed until the persecution ended and the bishops could meet; the council of 251 admitted certificate-buyers after penance and gave peace to those who had sacrificed only at the point of death; in 252, with a new persecution coming, his synod gave peace to all who had kept on repenting (Letter 53, modern 57). He was never lax. On the Lapsed 15-16 attacks quick readmission as 'a vain and false peace', and Letter 51.23 refuses peace to those who only ask for it when dying. On the Lapsed 36 says the true penitent 'shall make the Church which he had lately saddened glad, and shall now deserve of the Lord not only pardon, but a crown.' Letter 51.21 notes that some earlier African bishops 'wholly closed the gate of repentance against adultery' yet stayed in communion with the rest.

stances.summary: A bishop who had joined Novatian's schism came back weeping and confessing, and was received into communion as a layman. The whole congregation pleaded for him.
stances.quote: One of these bishops shortly after came back to the church, lamenting and confessing his transgression. And we communed with him as with a layman, all the people present interceding for him.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Letter to Fabius of Antioch, quoted by Eusebius, Church History
stances.context: Letter of 251. Here the fall is schism, not sacrifice, and the returning bishop is restored only as a layman. Cornelius also tells how confessors who had followed Novatian returned 'with lamentations and repentance' (6.43.6). Eusebius reports that Cornelius's Roman synod of sixty bishops decreed that the fallen should be healed 'with the medicines of repentance' (6.43.2; Eusebius's words). Cyprian confirms that Cornelius's council agreed with the African policy (Letter 51.6). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: The fallen who repent should not die shut out. I ordered that the dying be absolved when they asked, so they could leave this life with good hope.
stances.quote: But as I had commanded that persons at the point of death, if they requested it, and especially if they had asked for it previously, should receive remission, that they might depart with a good hope
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Letter to Fabius of Antioch, quoted by Eusebius, Church History
stances.context: c. 251. He tells of Serapion, an old believer who had sacrificed and begged in vain for absolution; on his deathbed his grandson brought him the Eucharist, and he died at once. Dionysius asks: 'Is it not evident that he was preserved and his life continued till he was absolved' (6.44.6). He also cites Alexandrian martyrs who themselves took the fallen back into 'prayers and feasts' and asks whether the church should overturn their mercy (6.42.5-6). He wrote letters On Repentance (6.46, lost) and urged Novatian to end the schism: 'it were better to suffer everything, rather than divide the Church of God' (6.45). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Receive back everyone who returns after any fall, whether it was a moral failure or a heresy.
stances.quote: commands them to receive those who come back again after any fall, whether it be delinquency or heresy.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Letter to the church of Amastris, summarized by Eusebius, Church History
stances.context: c. 170. This is Eusebius's summary of a lost letter, not Dionysius's own words. In another letter he urged Pinytus of Knossos not to lay 'a grievous and compulsory burden' of chastity on believers (4.23.7). Evidence that lenient practice is older than the third-century quarrels. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.person: The martyrs of Lyons and Vienne
stances.summary: The confessors in prison did not boast over those who had denied Christ. They wept and prayed for them, and many who had denied came back and confessed their faith.
stances.quote: For through their continued life the dead were made alive, and the witnesses showed favor to those who had failed to witness. And the virgin mother had much joy in receiving alive those whom she had brought forth as dead.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890
stances.work: Letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyons, quoted by Eusebius, Church History
stances.context: Written in 177. The 'virgin mother' is the Church. The letter says of the martyrs: 'They absolved all, but bound none' (5.2.5), and Eusebius adds that he records this against 'the inhuman and unmerciful disposition of those who, after these events, acted unsparingly toward the members of Christ' (5.2.8), probably the Novatianists. Here the fallen are restored by returning to confess under trial, not by a formal penance. A group, not one person.

stances.summary: After baptism there should be no more sin, but God in mercy has given one more repentance to those who fall. Only one: someone who keeps sinning and repenting will hardly live.
stances.quote: if any one is tempted by the devil, and sins after that great and holy calling in which the Lord has called His people to everlasting life, he has opportunity to repent but once. But if he should sin frequently after this, and then repent, to such a man his repentance will be of no avail; for with difficulty will he live.
stances.translation: F. Crombie, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Rome, early to mid 2nd century; widely read and treated as Scripture in some churches. Hermas offers this against 'some teachers' who said there is no repentance after baptism, and calls their teaching sound but not the whole story. In Mandate 4.1 a husband must take back an adulterous wife who repents, 'But not frequently. For there is but one repentance to the servants of God.' Because of this leniency the Montanist Tertullian called it the 'Shepherd of adulterers' (On Modesty 20).

stances.summary: God has left one more door open after baptism for those who fall. Knock and it will open, but only once. You have offended, but you can still be reconciled.
stances.quote: In the vestibule He has stationed the second repentance for opening to such as knock: but now once for all, because now for the second time; but never more because the last time it had been in vain.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: conlocavit in vestibulo paenitentiam secundam, quae pulsantibus patefaciat, sed iam semel quia iam secundo, sed amplius numquam quia proxime frustra.
stances.context: Written c. 203, in his Catholic period. The same chapter ends: 'You have offended, but can still be reconciled. You have One whom you may satisfy, and Him willing.' The second repentance is public (exomologesis): sackcloth, fasting, kneeling before the presbyters (ch. 9). It is once only. He later reversed himself for adultery, fornication, idolatry and murder: see his second stance. Latin from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.paen.shtml).

stances.summary: Whoever truly repents has a sure hope of salvation. The apostle John rode into the mountains after a young convert who had become a robber chief, and did not leave him until he had brought him back to the Church.
stances.quote: did not depart, as they say, till he restored him to the Church, presenting in him a great example of true repentance and a great token of regeneration, a trophy of the resurrection for which we hope
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
stances.context: c. 200. Clement calls the John story 'a narrative, handed down and committed to the custody of memory'. In Stromata 2.13 he limits this to one repentance after baptism: God 'has vouch-safed, in the case of those who, though in faith, fall into any transgression, a second repentance', but 'continual and successive repentings for sins differ nothing from the case of those who have not believed at all' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02102.htm).

stances.summary: Women led astray by the Gnostic teacher Marcus often came back to the Church, confessed their sins openly with tears, and were received.
stances.quote: At last, when, with no small difficulty, the brethren had converted her, she spent her whole time in the exercise of public confession, weeping over and lamenting the defilement which she had received from this magician.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: c. 180, describing practice in the Rhone valley. Those who returned did so, he says, 'a thing which frequently occurs' (1.13.5). Others, ashamed to confess openly, left entirely, 'despairing of [attaining to] the life of God' (1.13.7). Descriptive rather than argued: it shows public confession as the road back.

stances.summary: Those who confessed Christ and then denied Him are lost only if they never repent before death. God counts as righteous the one who repents.
stances.quote: such as have confessed and known this man to be Christ, yet who have gone back from some cause to the legal dispensation, and have denied that this man is Christ, and have repented not before death, shall by no means be saved.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: c. 155-160. The point is by implication: the apostate who does not repent before death is lost, and Justin at once adds that God's goodness holds 'righteous and sinless the man who, as Ezekiel tells, repents of sins'. He speaks of salvation, not of church discipline, and the apostasy in view is going back to the Jewish law.

stances.summary: The Lord forgives all who repent, if they come back to the unity of the Church and to communion with the bishop.
stances.quote: To all them that repent, the Lord grants forgiveness, if they turn in penitence to the unity of God, and to communion with the bishop.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: c. 107-110, on the road to martyrdom. He means those who followed schismatics or false teachers; chapter 3: 'as many as shall, in the exercise of repentance, return into the unity of the Church, these, too, shall belong to God'. Not about apostasy under persecution.

stances.summary: Valens, a presbyter who fell through greed, is to be grieved over and prayed for. Do not treat such people as enemies; call them back as sick and straying members.
stances.quote: but call them back as suffering and straying members, that you may save your whole body.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: c. 110-140. The sentence begins: 'And be then moderate in regard to this matter, and do not count such as enemies' (the page inserts a Bible reference, 2 Thessalonians 3:15, inside the sentence, so the quote starts after it). Polycarp calls avarice a form of idolatry and prays 'may the Lord grant true repentance' to Valens and his wife. This chapter survives only in Latin. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Those who have done penance for adultery and fornication are forgiven and may be restored.
stances.quote: The Pontifex Maximus — that is, the bishop of bishops — issues an edict: I remit, to such as have discharged (the requirements of) repentance, the sins both of adultery and of fornication.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.original: Pontifex scilicet maximus, episcopus episcoporum, edicit: « Ego et moechiae et fornicationis delicta paenitentia functis dimitto.
stances.work: A bishop's edict, quoted by Tertullian, On Modesty
stances.context: Tertullian quotes the edict in order to mock it and does not name the bishop. Older scholars took him to be Callistus of Rome (bishop c. 217-222), whom Hippolytus attacks for the same leniency; many now think of Agrippinus of Carthage or another African bishop. Treat the name as uncertain. This is the only surviving wording of the edict. Latin from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.pudicitia.shtml).

stances.summary: Christians mourn those who fall into grave sin as dead to God. If they truly change, they are received back as risen from the dead, after a longer trial than at first, but never again in church office.
stances.quote: the Christians lament as dead those who have been vanquished by licentiousness or any other sin, because they are lost and dead to God, and as being risen from the dead (if they manifest a becoming change) they receive them afterwards, at some future time, after a greater interval than in the case of those who were admitted at first
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: c. 248, describing Christian practice to a pagan critic. The sentence goes on: 'but not placing in any office or post of rank in the Church of God those who, after professing the Gospel, lapsed and fell.' Elsewhere Origen is stricter: in On Prayer 28 he blames priests who claim to pardon idolatry, adultery and fornication by their prayers (not quoted: no pre-1929 English checked). Origen's views on other matters were condemned in 553; he is not a saint.

stances.summary: No one who has turned to wrong, even under force, should despair. He can be brought back if he repents, as a father takes back a son he had disowned.
stances.quote: Nor, however, let any one be disheartened, or despair concerning himself, if, overcome by passion, or impelled by desire, or deceived by error, or compelled by force, he has turned aside to the way of unrighteousness. For it is possible for him to be brought back, and to be set free, if he repents of his actions, and, turning to better things, makes satisfaction to God.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written c. 304-311, during and after the Great Persecution, for educated pagans as well as Christians. It speaks of God's pardon, not of church procedure. The same chapter: 'if we think that our children are corrected when we perceive that they repent of their faults, and though we have disinherited and cast them off, we again receive, cherish, and embrace them, why should we despair that the mercy of God our Father may again be appeased by repentance?'

stances.summary: When a monastery refused to take back a monk who had fallen, Antony sent word: a ship that lost its cargo in a storm has barely reached land; do you want to drown the one who was saved? They took him back.
stances.quote: Do ye wish to drown him that hath been saved?
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac)
stances.original: ὑμεῖς δὲ τὰ σωθέντα ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν θέλετε καταποντίσαι
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers)
stances.location: no. 606 in Budge's numbering; Greek alphabetical collection, Antony 21
stances.context: Budge translates the Syriac collection of Anan-Isho (7th century), which draws on the 5th-century Sayings. The url is archive.org's OCR text of the 1907 book: Budge prints a quotation mark at the start of each line of speech, and the OCR has double spaces and misreadings such as 'AbbA'. The monastery is that of 'Abba Hatil (or Helit)', Elias in the Greek. The full message reads: 'A storm rose up against a ship on the sea, and destroyed the freight which she carried, but with the greatest difficulty she was saved [and brought] to land. Now what do ye wish to do? Do ye wish to drown him that hath been saved?' The next saying (607) has Antony say it is better to fall and rise than to stand and then fall. The Greek original field is the parallel line in the Greek alphabetical collection ('you want to sink in the sea what was saved onto land'), from http://www.ldysinger.com/@texts/0400_apophth/greek_alph/01_Introd_alpha-gamma.htm (that page's English is Benedicta Ward's, copyrighted, not used).

stances.summary: When the brothers met to judge a monk who had sinned, Moses came carrying a leaking basket of sand. My own sins run out behind me where I cannot see them, he said, and I have come to judge someone else's. They let the brother go.
stances.quote: [The sands are] my sins "which are running down behind me and I cannot see them, "and I, even I, have come this day to judge shortcomings
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers)
stances.location: no. 542 in Budge's numbering; Greek alphabetical collection, Moses 2
stances.context: The stray quotation marks inside the quote are Budge's running quotation marks, kept because the quote is copied exactly from the OCR page. The sentence ends after a page break: 'which are not mine.' Clean reading: '[The sands are] my sins which are running down behind me and I cannot see them, and I, even I, have come this day to judge shortcomings which are not mine.' Then 'they set free that brother and said nothing [further] to him.' Indirect evidence: the story is about refusing to condemn a sinning brother, not about a formal return after penance.

stances.summary: A brother asked how long to do penance for a great sin: three years? one year? forty days? Poemen said each was too much. If a man repents with his whole heart and stops, God receives him in three days.
stances.quote: I say that if a man repents with his whole heart, and does not go on to do the sin again, God receives him even within three days.
stances.translation: own literal rendering from the Greek (alphabetical collection, as printed at the url)
stances.original: Ἐγὼ λέγω͵ ὅτι ἐὰν ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας μετανοήσῃ ἄνθρωπος͵ καὶ μὴ προσθῇ ἔτι ποιεῖν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν͵ καὶ εἰς τρεῖς ἡμέρας δέχεται αὐτὸν ὁ Θεός
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: Only modern English exists (Benedicta Ward, 1975, copyrighted; it is printed on the same page and was not used). The Greek page uses the sign ͵ where a comma stands. Poemen is arguing against long fixed penances, not against discipline as such. In Budge's Syriac-based collection (no. 609) Poemen also says he prefers a man who has sinned and repented to one who has not sinned and shows no repentance, because the first is humble.

stances.summary: Those who were pulled into the Arian party under pressure, and repent, are to be pardoned. Ringleaders are pardoned too but lose clerical rank; those forced by violence may keep it.
stances.quote: in the case of those who had fallen and been leaders of impiety, to pardon them upon their repentance, but not to give them the position of clergy: but in the case of men not deliberate in impiety, but drawn away by necessity and violence, that they should not only receive pardon, but should occupy the position of clergy
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: c. 362-363, reporting the decision of the Council of Alexandria (362) and of like councils in Greece, Spain and Gaul. The fall here is into heresy under imperial pressure, not pagan sacrifice. Athanasius endorses the decision.

stances.summary: Never despair of being saved. God forgives fornication, adultery and sins done many times; Peter denied Christ three times and was forgiven and kept his place as an apostle.
stances.quote: Let us not despair of ourselves, brethren; let us not abandon ourselves to a hopeless condition. For it is a fearful thing not to believe in a hope of repentance.
stances.translation: Edwin Hamilton Gifford, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: c. 350, to candidates for baptism, so much of it concerns sins before baptism; but his examples include Peter's denial, forgiven with 'his Apostolic dignity unforfeited' (2.19). Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Those who denied Christ under torture may come back after years of graded penance. What matters is not the length of time but the fruit of repentance.
stances.quote: Those who have endured grievous tortures and have been forced to denial, through inability to sustain the anguish, may be excluded for three years, hearers for two, kneelers for three, and so be received into communion.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 8, 1895
stances.context: 375. Penance is long and graded: murder twenty years (56), adultery fifteen (58). One who has deliberately 'denied Christ' is to weep all his life and receive the sacrament only at death, 'through faith in the mercy of God' (73). Yet: 'I do not decide such matters absolutely by time, but I give heed to the manner of penance' (84). So Basil takes the penitent back, slowly; for deliberate apostasy, only at death. Basil's canons became church law in the East.

stances.summary: Refusing pardon to penitents kills repentance itself, because no one can repent well without hope of mercy. Christ gave His Church the power to loose as well as to bind.
stances.quote: For what is more harsh than to inflict a penance which they do not relax, and by refusing pardon to take away the incentive to penance and repentance? Now no one can repent to good purpose unless he hopes for mercy.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896
stances.context: c. 384-390, a two-book treatise against the Novatianists. To Novatian: 'It would be more endurable, Novatian, that you should forgive than that you should bind' (1.2.9). But public penance happens once: 'as there is but one baptism, so there is but one course of penance, so far as the outward practice goes' (2.10.95), and he says he found it easier to meet the innocent than those who had repented fittingly (2.10.96). He practised it: he required public penance of Emperor Theodosius after the massacre at Thessalonica (390) and then received him back.

stances.summary: Offering the cure of repentance again does not teach people to sin, any more than rescuing a shipwrecked man drives him onto the rocks. The Church may forgive the penitent and receive him.
stances.quote: God wisheth not man to sin even once, and yet He delivers him from sin. Nor yet when He delivereth, doth He teach sin; as neither does he who delivers from a fire, teach to kindle it; nor does he who rescues the shipwrecked from the cliffs, drive him upon the rocks.
stances.translation: C. H. Collyns, Library of the Fathers vol. 17, 1842
stances.work: Letter 3 to Sympronian (Against the treatise of the Novatians)
stances.context: Pacian, bishop of Barcelona (died before 392), wrote three letters to the Novatianist Sympronian and an Exhortation to Penance. He is answering the objection 'If God bids man often repent, He allows him often to sin' (3.21). Not in the candidate pool, but the most sustained Western answer to the rigorists after Cyprian.

stances.summary: Refuse the unrepentant, yes. But if someone wears himself out with weeping, receive him and give him his proper place. Novatian's lack of mercy is no rule for me.
stances.quote: If they were unrepentant he was right; I too would refuse to receive those who either would not stoop at all or not sufficiently, and who would refuse to make their amendment counterbalance their sin; and when I do receive them, I will assign them their proper place; but if he refused those who wore themselves away with weeping, I will not imitate him.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached at Epiphany in Constantinople, 381, to an audience that included Novatianists. In 39.18: 'For both are alike evil, indulgence not regulated by prudence, and condemnation that will never forgive; the one because it relaxes all reins, the other because it strangles by its severity.' He cites Peter's denial, David, and the sinner at Corinth whom Paul restored.

stances.summary: Fabiola, who had remarried after divorcing her husband, stood among the penitents before all Rome and was restored to communion. No sin is beyond the reach of tears like hers.
stances.quote: What sins would such a penance fail to purge away? What ingrained stains would such tears be unable to wash out?
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: c. 399, on the death of Fabiola. Jerome counted her second marriage as a serious sin; she was 'Restored to communion before the eyes of the whole church' (77.6) and then founded a hospital. In the Dialogue against the Luciferians (c. 379) his spokesman argues that bishops who fell into Arianism at Ariminum and repented should be received back, against rigorists who would accept them only as laymen. He urges a fallen deacon to 'clutch the plank' after shipwreck (Letter 147.3).

stances.summary: Have you sinned? Come into the church and repent, and if you fall again, repent again. The church is a place of healing, not a law court.
stances.quote: Have you sinned? Go into the church and wipe out your sin. [...] Even if you sin a second time, repent a second time. [...] For this is a place of healing, not a law court. It does not demand an account for sins; it grants forgiveness of sins.
stances.translation: own literal rendering from the Greek (Migne, PG 49.297-298)
stances.original: Ἥμαρτες; [...] εἴσελθε εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, καὶ ἐξάλειψόν σου τὴν ἁμαρτίαν. [...] κἂν δεύτερον ἁμάρτῃς, δεύτερον μετανόησον [...] ἰατρεῖον γάρ ἐστιν ἐνταῦθα, οὐ δικαστήριον, οὐκ εὐθύνας ἁμαρτημάτων ἀπαιτοῦν, ἀλλὰ συγχώρησιν [49.298] ἁμαρτημάτων παρέχον.
stances.location: Homily 3, On almsgiving and the ten virgins (PG 49.297-298)
stances.context: Antioch, late 380s. The only English is modern (FOTC 1998), so the rendering is my own. The Greek page prints a line number between every sentence and the Migne column marker [49.298] inside the last sentence; [...] marks where the page prints a line number or where lines are skipped. Of this set of homilies, Homily 7 is spurious; Homily 3 is not among those I found disputed. Contemporaries thought him too lax: Socrates (Church History 6.21) says the synod of bishops allowed repentance only once after baptism, but 'he did not scruple to say, Approach, although you may have repented a thousand times', and the Novatianist bishop Sisinnius wrote a book against it. In public-domain English his first letter to the fallen Theodore says the same: 'He never turns his face away from a sincere repentance' (1.6) and 'For even if you should despair of yourself ten thousand times, I will never despair of you' (1.15) (W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF 1st series vol. 9, 1889, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1903.htm). Theodore's 'fall' was leaving monastic life to marry and practise law. This homily is the real source behind the modern saying that the church is a hospital: see misattributions.

stances.summary: Even the greatest crimes can be forgiven in the Church. No one who truly repents should despair of God's mercy; the depth of sorrow matters more than the length of time.
stances.quote: But even crimes themselves, however great, may be remitted in the Holy Church; and the mercy of God is never to be despaired of by men who truly repent, each according to the measure of his sin.
stances.translation: J. F. Shaw, NPNF 1st series vol. 3, 1887
stances.context: c. 421. He adds that bishops rightly fix times of penance because sorrow cannot be seen, and that to refuse to believe, to the end, that sins are forgiven in the Church is the unforgivable sin (ch. 83). In Letter 153.7 (to Macedonius, 414) he notes the rule that the humblest public penance is granted only once (checked in secondary sources only; not quoted). Against the Donatists he argued for receiving returning schismatics.

stances.summary: Old sins are washed away by a better life, and those who stop sinning are to be absolved by God's mercy. Martin took back monks who had fallen, and told the devil himself that if he repented, Martin would promise him Christ's mercy.
stances.quote: Martin, resisting the devil firmly, answered him, that by-past sins are cleansed away by the leading of a better life, and that through the mercy of God, those are to be absolved from their sins who have given up their evil ways.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894
stances.original: Martinum diabolo repugnantem respondisse constanter, antiqua delicta melioris vitae conversatione purgari, et per misericordiam Domini absolvendos esse peccatis, qui peccare desierint.
stances.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St. Martin
stances.context: Sulpicius knew Martin personally and wrote before Martin's death (c. 396). The words are reported by brothers who overheard; the devil voices the rigorist case, that 'no mercy was extended by the Lord to those who had once fallen away'. Martin: 'If you, yourself, wretched being, would but desist from attacking mankind... I, with a true confidence in the Lord, would promise you the mercy of Christ.' The monks he took back had 'lost their baptism by falling into various errors'. Latin from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/sulpiciusseverusmartin.html).

stances.summary: A monk who leaves through his own fault may be taken back if he promises to amend, at the lowest rank, and up to three times. After that the door is closed.
stances.quote: if he wish to return, shall first promise every amends for the fault on account of which he departed; and thus he shall be received into the lowest degree—so that thereby his humility may be proved. But if he again depart, up to the third time he shall be received. Knowing that after this every opportunity of return is denied to him.
stances.translation: Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages, 1892
stances.original: Frater qui proprio vitio egreditur de monasterio, si reverti voluerit, spondeat prius omnem emendationem pro quo egressus est, et sic in ultimo gradu recipiatur, ut ex hoc eius humilitas conprobetur. Quod si denuo exierit, usque tertio ita recipiatur, iam postea sciens omnem sibi reversionis aditum denegari.
stances.context: c. 530-560. Leaving the monastery breaks a vow; it is not denying the faith. Chapters 27-28 tell the abbot to care for excommunicated brothers like a wise physician and the Good Shepherd, but to cut off the incorrigible. Latin from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/benedict.html).

stances.summary: The fallen may knock at the Church's door, but they must wait at the threshold until a council of bishops decides. Meanwhile only the truly penitent who are dying should be helped, and God will judge them.
stances.quote: Let them indeed knock at the doors, but assuredly let them not break them down; let them present themselves at the threshold of the church, but certainly let them not leap over it
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: Letter 30 in Cyprian's correspondence (the Roman clergy to Cyprian), written by Novatian
stances.context: Written in 250 while the see of Rome was vacant. Cyprian says Novatian wrote it and read it aloud, and that it granted peace to the lapsed 'who were sick and at the point of departure' (Letter 51.5). It already stresses severity ('Far be it from the Roman Church to slacken her vigour', 30.3) but allows cautious help to dying penitents (30.8). This is the view he later abandoned: see his second stance. Novatian became a schismatic in 251; his work On the Trinity is orthodox.

stances.summary: Those who sacrificed to idols must not be readmitted to Communion. Urge them to repent, but leave their pardon to God alone.
stances.quote: they should not admit to the sacred mysteries those who had sacrificed; but exhorting them to repentance, leave the pardoning of their offense to God, who has the power to forgive all sin.
stances.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF 2nd series vol. 2, 1890
stances.work: Circular letter to the churches, as quoted by Socrates Scholasticus, Church History
stances.context: From 251, after Cornelius was elected bishop of Rome. Novatian's own letters on this are lost; Socrates quotes this sentence about 190 years later and was friendly to the Novatianists. Contemporaries report the same view: Eusebius says he held there was no hope for them 'not even if they should do all things pertaining to a genuine and pure conversion' (Church History 6.43.1); Cyprian mocks a teaching that says 'Mourn and shed tears, and groan day and night... but, after all these things, you shall die without the pale of the Church' (Letter 51.28); Ambrose says Novatian 'thought that no one should be admitted to penance' (On Repentance 1.3.10). Rigorists did not deny that God might forgive; they denied that the Church could restore. Schismatic. This reverses his own earlier letter (see his mixed stance).

stances.summary: The Church must not promise pardon to adulterers and fornicators. They may weep before its doors all their lives, and God may forgive them, but the Church will not take them back.
stances.quote: The self-same liminal limit we fix for adulterers also and fornicators; dooming them to pour forth tears barren of peace, and to regain from the Church no ampler return than the publication of their disgrace.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.original: Eundem limitem liminis moechis quoque et fornicatoribus figimus ieiunas pacis lacrimas profusuris nec amplius ab ecclesia quam publicationem dedecoris relaturis.
stances.context: Written c. 210-220, as a Montanist, against a bishop's edict that pardoned sexual sins after penance. He admits a change of mind and says he blushes 'not at an error which I have ceased to hold' (ch. 1). The penitent's tears are not wasted: repentance 'gains it by entreaty from God alone' and 'prefers the blush of shame to the privilege of communion' (ch. 3). He cites a Montanist oracle: 'The Church has the power to forgive sins; but I will not do it, lest they commit others withal' (ch. 21; Latin 'Potest ecclesia donare delictum, sed non faciam, ne et alia delinquant'). He calls Hermas 'the only one which favours adulterers' (ch. 10) and 'that apocryphal Shepherd of adulterers' (ch. 20). Heterodox (Montanist). This reverses On Repentance 7 (see his agree stance). Latin from The Latin Library.

stances.summary: A bishop who announces that he forgives everyone's sins of the flesh is not healing sinners but indulging them, and he fills his church with people rightly expelled.
stances.quote: And he first invented the device of conniving with men in regard of their indulgence in sensual pleasures, saying that all had their sins forgiven by himself.
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.location: Book 9, chapter 7 in the ANF (9.12 in modern editions)
stances.context: Written c. 225-235 against Callistus of Rome, his rival. He also objects that Callistus used the parable of the tares and Noah's ark, with 'dogs, and wolves, and ravens, and all things clean and unclean', to argue 'let those who in the Church are guilty of sin remain in it'. This shows Hippolytus against lenient readmission, but it is a polemic against a rival, and he nowhere says that no penitent may ever return. Use with care. He was later reconciled and died a martyr with Pontian (c. 235); venerated as a saint.

stances.summary: Those who commit a deadly sin after baptism must not receive the sacraments again. Urge them to repent, but they must look for forgiveness from God, not from a priest.
stances.quote: that they should indeed be exhorted to repentance, but were not to expect remission from the priest, but from God, who is able and has authority to forgive sins.
stances.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF 2nd series vol. 2, 1890
stances.work: Reported by Socrates Scholasticus, Church History
stances.context: Acesius, Novatianist bishop at Constantinople, was invited to the Council of Nicaea (325). He accepted its creed and Easter date but not readmission. Emperor Constantine answered: 'Place a ladder, Acesius, and climb alone into heaven.' Socrates says he heard this from Auxanon, a Novatianist presbyter who went to Nicaea with Acesius as a youth (1.10, 1.13), and that Eusebius does not mention it. Reported speech, written down about a century later. Schismatic.

stances.summary: Chrysostom's promise that sinners may come back to church however many times they have repented is wrong and dangerous.
stances.quote: he did not scruple to say, 'Approach, although you may have repented a thousand times.' For this doctrine, many even of his friends censured him, but especially Sisinnius bishop of the Novatian; who wrote a book condemnatory of the above quoted expression of Chrysostom's, and severely rebuked him for it.
stances.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF 2nd series vol. 2, 1890
stances.work: Reported by Socrates Scholasticus, Church History
stances.context: Sisinnius was Novatianist bishop of Constantinople around 400; Socrates admires his learning (6.22). His book is lost; this is Socrates's report, which also says many of Chrysostom's own friends censured the saying and that the synod of bishops allowed repentance after baptism only once. Novatianists refused readmission for grave sins altogether, so his objection went further than the once-only rule. Schismatic.

stances.summary: There is no repentance after baptism for grave sin. The Church cannot forgive mortal sin, and it corrupts itself if it takes sinners back.
stances.quote: That there is no room for repentance after Baptism; that the Church cannot remit mortal sin; that by the receiving of sinners she herself perishes.
stances.translation: C. H. Collyns, Library of the Fathers vol. 17, 1842
stances.work: His lost treatise, summarized by Pacian of Barcelona, Letter 3 to Sympronian
stances.context: A Novatianist layman or teacher in Spain in the later 4th century. His treatise is lost; these are Pacian's words summarizing it in order to refute it, so treat the wording as Pacian's. Pacian's letter quotes several of Sympronian's arguments directly, such as 'If God bids man often repent, He allows him often to sin' (3.21). Schismatic.

splits_fathers: Strongly one-sided in favour of taking the penitent back. Every voice in the candidate pool that I could prove on this question says yes, in some form: Hermas, Clement, Cyprian, Origen, Lactantius, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine, Martin, Antony, Moses, Poemen and Benedict; the councils agree (Nicaea, canons 8 and 11-14). But there are real voices on the other side: Tertullian in his Montanist years (On Modesty), Novatian from 251 and the Novatianist church that lasted into the fifth century (Acesius at Nicaea, Sympronian in Spain, Sisinnius at Constantinople), Hippolytus against Callistus (by implication), the earlier African bishops who "wholly closed the gate of repentance against adultery" (Cyprian, Letter 51.21), and the Council of Elvira (c. 306), whose first canon, as quoted in secondary sources, denies communion even at death to a baptized adult who sacrifices to idols. The rigorists did not say God cannot forgive; they said the Church may not restore. Among the majority the live disagreements are sharper and more useful for a quiz. HOW OFTEN: once only (Hermas, Clement, the early Tertullian, Ambrose's "one course of penance", the synod rule Socrates reports) or again and again (Chrysostom, whom contemporaries called lax for it). HOW LONG: Basil's fifteen to twenty years, or communion only at death for deliberate apostasy, against Poemen's "three days" if the heart is whole. ONLY AT DEATH OR IN LIFE: Cyprian's first stage, Basil canon 73 and Elvira against Dionysius's and Cyprian's later practice. WHETHER A FALLEN LEADER GETS HIS OFFICE BACK: no for Origen, Cornelius, Athanasius (for ringleaders) and the Luciferians (for bishops); yes for the coerced in Athanasius and in Jerome's dialogue. Cyprian, Novatian and Tertullian each changed their minds on this question, in different directions.
splits_people_today: As worded, the claim is close to one-sided today. Most Christians of every tradition, and most non-religious people who value second chances, would agree that someone truly sorry should be welcomed back. Almost no one now argues that a repentant adulterer, or a Christian who once renounced the faith under pressure, must be shut out for life. So the bare claim will tell the quiz little. Real splits appear as soon as one condition is added. (1) Repeat failure: many people say "forgive, but not endlessly" (the Hermas and Ambrose view), others say "seventy times seven" (Chrysostom). (2) Proof and time: some want visible change over a long period before trust returns (Basil, Cyprian), others think a sincere heart is enough at once (Poemen). (3) Getting a position back: whether a fallen pastor, priest or leader should return to the pulpit splits congregations sharply today, and the common "welcome back as a member, not as a leader" answer is Origen's, Cornelius's and Athanasius's. (4) Grave harm to others, such as abuse, violence or betraying a community under pressure: here many people, religious or not, say some acts should bar a person for good even if they are sorry, which is the Novatianist instinct in modern form. The church frame is also narrower than people use today; everyday versions of the same question (taking back a friend, a spouse, an employee) divide people more evenly than church membership does.

misattributions.line: The church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints.
misattributions.truth: No patristic source is known. Secondary sources trace the wording to a 1964 'Dear Abby' column by Abigail Van Buren (Pauline Phillips); I did not check that column. The nearest genuine patristic line is Chrysostom, Homilies on Repentance 3 (PG 49.297-298): the church is 'a place of healing, not a law court' (ἰατρεῖον γάρ ἐστιν ἐνταῦθα, οὐ δικαστήριον). It is recorded in this file under Chrysostom. Quote that, not the museum line.

misattributions.line: Every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.
misattributions.truth: Oscar Wilde, A Woman of No Importance (1893), Act 3: 'The only difference between the saint and the sinner is that every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.' Checked in the Project Gutenberg text (ebook 854). Not a Father.

misattributions.line: Approach, although you may have repented a thousand times.
misattributions.truth: A report by a historian writing about forty years later who was friendly to the Novatianists. I did not find these words, or any 'thousand times' line, in the Greek of the Homilies on Repentance on the Documenta Catholica Omnia page. The genuine line with the same sense is Homily 3: 'even if you sin a second time, repent a second time'. Quote the homily, or cite Socrates as Socrates.

notes:
LEADS CHECKED. Cyprian's letter to Antonianus is Letter 51 in the ANF numbering used by New Advent (55 in modern editions); section 29 carries the position, sections 3-7 his change of mind. Novatian's own voice survives only in Letter 30 (his moderate view of 250, attested as his by Cyprian, Letter 51.5); his later rigorist wording survives only as quoted by Socrates (4.28) and as described by opponents. Cornelius's letter is Eusebius 6.43; Dionysius on Serapion is 6.44, and his letter to Novatian 6.45. Hermas, Mandate 4.3, holds (one repentance). Tertullian, On Repentance 7-9, holds. "Shepherd of adulterers" is On Modesty 20 (Latin "illo apocrypho Pastore moechorum"), not chapter 10; chapter 10 has "the only one which favours adulterers" ("quae sola moechos amat"). Hippolytus against Callistus is Refutation 9.7 in the ANF (9.12 in modern Greek editions). Ambrose, On Repentance, and Pacian's letters to Sympronian hold. Chrysostom's Letters to Theodore hold (NPNF 1.9); his Homilies on Repentance have only modern English, so the key line is my own rendering from the Greek. Basil's relevant canons are in Letter 217 (canons 56, 58, 73, 81, 84), not 188 or 199.

NOT USED, AND WHY. Origen, On Prayer 28 and Homilies on Leviticus 15.2 (stricter lines), and Augustine, Letter 153.7 (public penance only once): no pre-1929 English checked, so they appear in context only. Gregory of Nyssa's Canonical Letter to Letoius (lifelong penance for voluntary apostasy): not verified, no public-domain English found. Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule III.29-30 is about personal repentance, not readmission. Isaac the Syrian: the only old English (Wensinck) has an uncertain public-domain date. Ephrem's Homily on Admonition and Repentance (NPNF 2.13) does not touch readmission. No usable evidence found for Macrina, Syncletica, Arsenius, Evagrius, Hilary, Paulinus, Cassian, Boethius, Climacus or Pelagius on this question.

SOURCE FORMAT WARNINGS. The Antony and Moses quotes are copied from archive.org's OCR text of Budge (1907). Budge prints a quotation mark at the start of every line of speech, so the Moses quote contains stray quotation marks; a clean reading is in its context. The Chrysostom and Poemen stances are own renderings. Their "original" fields are copied from the Greek pages: Chrysostom's pieces are joined with [...] because the page prints a line number between sentences, and [49.298] is Migne's column marker printed on the page; Poemen's page uses the sign ͵ as a comma. New Advent's ANF and NPNF texts are lightly revised by its editor (for example "you" for "thou").

WHO IS "FARTHEST". For a player who says no, the clearly named opponents are Novatian (later stance) and Tertullian (Montanist stance). Acesius has the most memorable exchange on the strict side (Constantine: "Place a ladder, Acesius, and climb alone into heaven"), but it was written down a century later. For a player who says yes, the most vivid lines are Chrysostom ("a place of healing, not a law court"), Antony (the ship saved from the storm), Poemen ("three days") and Martin (mercy promised even to the devil). Cyprian is the best "yes, but": received after long, real penance, never on a deathbed request alone. Cyprian, Novatian and Tertullian all changed their minds; Novatian and Tertullian each have two stances.

HETERODOX AND DISPUTED. Tertullian's On Modesty is Montanist. Novatian, Acesius, Sisinnius and Sympronian were schismatics (Novatianist). Origen's teachings on other matters were condemned in 553. Hippolytus opposed Callistus as a rival bishop but is venerated as a martyr. The bishop of Tertullian's edict is unnamed; "Callistus" is a scholarly guess. The martyrs of Lyons are a group, not one person. Dionysius of Corinth's stance is Eusebius's summary, not his words; Sympronian's is Pacian's summary.
